summary: This document defines two MIB modules containing textual conventions for commonly used Bidirectional Forwarding Detection management information. Other BFD-related MIB modules can import these definitions instead of each inventing their own.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people fill out forms, it helps to agree on one way to write dates. This RFC sets shared formats for describing BFD settings so every management tool uses the same ones.

questions: which udp ports does bfd use
what are the bfd session states
subtitle: Shared data-type definitions so every BFD management module describes intervals, ports and states the same way.

tldr.problem: Every MIB module that manages Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) would otherwise invent its own way to represent things like session indexes, intervals and diagnostic codes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7330 defines two MIB modules of textual conventions, one BFD-specific (BFD-TC-STD-MIB) and one maintained by IANA (IANA-BFD-TC-STD-MIB), for other BFD MIB modules to import.
tldr.outcome: BFD MIB modules can share one set of types, and new IANA-managed values can be added through IETF Review without republishing the RFC.

today: RFC 7330 is a Proposed Standard from August 2014 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is imported by the BFD MIB in RFC 7331.

sections.title: Why Shared Textual Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 7330 defines two MIB (Management Information Base) modules that hold textual conventions (TCs) for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD). A textual convention is a named, reusable data type with its own meaning and value range. The intent is that BFD-related MIB modules import these types instead of defining their own representations.

Names are prefixed to show where they come from: Bfd for types specific to BFD modules and IANA for types that IANA maintains. The module is written in SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP like any other MIB. For BFD itself, the RFC points to RFC 5880, RFC 5881, RFC 5883, RFC 6428 and RFC 7130.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a class agreeing that 'a score' always means a number from 1 to 10. Then every worksheet means the same thing.

sections.title: The BFD Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The first module, BFD-TC-STD-MIB, defines five types:

  • BfdSessIndexTC: an index that uniquely identifies a BFD session, from 1 to 4294967295.
  • BfdIntervalTC: a BFD interval in microseconds, from 0 to 4294967295.
  • BfdMultiplierTC: the failure detection multiplier, from 1 to 255.
  • BfdCtrlDestPortNumberTC: the UDP destination port of BFD control packets.
  • BfdCtrlSourcePortNumberTC: the UDP source port of BFD control packets.

All of them are based on Unsigned32 and use the display hint d, which means they are shown as plain decimal numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the labelled boxes for the basics: which session, how often to check, how many missed checks mean trouble, and which door (port) the messages use.

sections.title: Port Numbers and Their Open Range
sections.content:
The destination port type documents three well-known values: 3784 for a single-hop BFD session, 4784 for a multi-hop session and 6784 for BFD on a Link Aggregation Group (LAG). These come from RFC 5881, RFC 5883 and RFC 7130.

The syntax is still left open to the full range 0..65535 on purpose, for two stated reasons: an implementation may use a non-compliant port number for a valid proprietary reason, and future extension documents may need other values. The value 0 is a special reserved value for special conditions and should not be considered a valid port number. The source port type follows the same open-range logic and cites the port range 49152..65535 from RFC 5881.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule says which doors people normally use, but it does not nail the other doors shut in case someone needs one later.

sections.title: The IANA-Maintained Types
sections.content:
The second module, IANA-BFD-TC-STD-MIB, holds enumerated types whose values IANA controls. There are six:

  • IANAbfdDiagTC: a diagnostic code, noDiagnostic(0) through misConnectivityDefect(9). Examples are controlDetectionTimeExpired(1), echoFunctionFailed(2), neighborSignaledSessionDown(3) and administrativelyDown(7).
  • IANAbfdSessTypeTC: singleHop(1) and three multi-hop kinds (arbitrary paths, out-of-band signaling, unidirectional links).
  • IANAbfdSessOperModeTC: asynchronous or demand mode, each with or without the echo function (values 1 to 4).
  • IANAbfdSessStateTC: adminDown(1), down(2), init(3), up(4) and failing(5). The failing(5) state applies only to a session running BFD version 0.
  • IANAbfdSessAuthenticationTypeTC: from noAuthentication(-1) and simplePassword(1) up to meticulousKeyedSHA1(5).
  • IANAbfdSessAuthenticationKeyTC: an octet string of 0 to 252 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the official lists, like a menu of reasons a link went down or kinds of password checks, kept by the people who hand out Internet numbers.

sections.title: Authentication Type and Key Together
sections.content:
The key type is always read in the context of an authentication type value, and every use of the type convention must name the key object that provides that context. The key must be consistent with the type, and setting an inconsistent value must fail with an inconsistentValue error.

The size limits per type are: noAuthentication(-1) and reserved(0) have size 0; simplePassword(1) is 1 to 16 octets; keyedMD5(2) and meticulousKeyedMD5(3) are 16 octets; keyedSHA1(4) and meticulousKeyedSHA1(5) are 20 octets.

If the key type is used as an index, SMIv2's limit of 128 sub-identifiers can become a problem. In that case the object definition MUST include a SIZE clause, or the constraints must be stated in the row description.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock and its key must match. A small key does not fit a big lock, so the rules say how long the key must be for each kind of lock.

sections.title: Security and IANA Control
sections.content:
The document defines no management objects, only conventions. Meaningful security considerations can therefore only be written in the MIB modules that define objects, and the RFC says it has no impact on the security of the Internet.

The IANA module is under the direct control of IANA, and assignments are made through IETF Review (RFC 5226). IANA assigned { mib-2 223 } to BFD-TC-STD-MIB and { mib-2 224 } to IANA-BFD-TC-STD-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only makes the labels, not the controls, so it cannot be misused by itself. The real safety rules live in the documents that use the labels.
